journal: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
title: Object detection from UAV thermal infrared images and videos using YOLO models
categories: Journal: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
summary: Object detection is one of the most crucial tasks in computer vision and remote sensing to identify specific categories of various objects in images. The unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based thermal infrared (TIR) remote sensing multi-scenario images and videos are two important data sources in public security. However, their object detection process is still challenging because of the complicated scene information, coarse resolution compared with the visible videos and lack of public labelled datasets and training models. This study proposed a UAV TIR object detection framework for images and videos. The You Only Look Once (YOLO) models based on Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture were designed to extract features from ground-based TIR images and videos, which were captured by Forward-looking Infrared (FLIR) cameras. The most effective algorithm was finally identified by evaluation metrics and then applied to detect objects on TIR videos from UAVs. Results showed that the highest mean average precision (mAP) of the person and car instances was 88.69% in the validating task. The fastest detection speed achieved 50 frames per second (FPS), and the smallest model size was observed in YOLOv5-s. In the application, the cross-detection performance on persons and cars in UAV TIR videos under a YOLOv5-s model was discussed in terms of the different UAVs’ observation angles and the effectiveness of the YOLO architecture was revealed. This study provides positive support for the qualitative and quantitative evaluation of objection detection from TIR images and videos using deep-learning models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a UAV thermal-infrared object detection framework using CNN-based YOLO models, identifies YOLOv5-s as the smallest and fastest (50 FPS) variant with a highest mAP of 88.69% for person/car detection, and evaluates cross-detection across UAV observation angles.
AI.research_relevance: Moderate. The paper directly combines remote sensing (UAV TIR) with object detection (person/car) and touches on model efficiency via YOLO variant selection (smallest model, 50 FPS). However, it does not address satellite/aerial imagery, oriented boxes, small-target-specific design, or any real deployment/lightweighting technique (pruning, quantization, distillation, NAS). Its relevance to onboard satellite lightweighting is indirect and mostly motivational.
AI.task_and_scene: Task: object detection in UAV-based thermal infrared (TIR) images and videos for public-security applications. Scene: multi-scenario ground-based and UAV TIR data. Sensor/modality: thermal infrared captured by Forward-looking Infrared (FLIR) cameras. Target classes: persons and cars.
AI.model_architecture: CNN-based YOLO models (You Only Look Once) designed to extract features from ground-based TIR images and videos. The abstract names YOLOv5-s explicitly as the smallest model; other YOLO variants are compared but not individually enumerated. No architectural details (backbone, neck, head, anchor design) are provided.
AI.lightweight_method: The lightweighting evidence is limited to model-size comparison among YOLO variants: YOLOv5-s is reported as the smallest model and achieves the fastest detection speed (50 FPS). No pruning, quantization, knowledge distillation, NAS, or explicit parameter/FLOPs reporting is mentioned. The abstract does not specify any compression or acceleration techniques beyond selecting a smaller YOLO variant.
AI.onboard_deployability: Limited. The abstract reports 50 FPS detection speed and smallest model size for YOLOv5-s, but does not specify the hardware on which these were measured, nor parameters, FLOPs, memory, or energy. There is no evidence of deployment on edge devices, FPGAs, NPUs, or onboard/in-orbit platforms. The 50 FPS figure is therefore not verifiable as an onboard real-time capability.
AI.datasets_and_metrics: UAV-based thermal infrared (TIR) images and videos captured by Forward-looking Infrared (FLIR) cameras, including multi-scenario public-security data. Metrics: mean average precision (mAP), detection speed in FPS, and model size. The abstract reports a highest mAP of 88.69% for person and car instances in the validating task, fastest detection at 50 FPS, and smallest model size in YOLOv5-s. Specific dataset names, split sizes, and evaluation protocols are not stated.
AI.experiments: The study compares multiple YOLO models (CNN-based) on ground-based TIR images/videos, identifies the most effective algorithm by evaluation metrics, and then applies it to UAV TIR videos. Reported results: highest mAP of 88.69% for person and car instances in validation; fastest detection speed 50 FPS; smallest model size observed in YOLOv5-s. Cross-detection performance on persons and cars in UAV TIR videos under YOLOv5-s is discussed across different UAV observation angles. No baseline details, ablation studies, or per-class breakdowns are reported in the abstract.
AI.limitations: Abstract does not specify: exact dataset names/sizes, per-class mAP, parameter counts, FLOPs, latency, memory footprint, energy consumption, or any edge/embedded hardware deployment. The 50 FPS and model-size claims are not tied to a specific hardware platform, so real-time capability on onboard/edge devices cannot be verified. The study targets UAV TIR (person/car) rather than satellite/aerial object detection, and no oriented bounding boxes or small-target-specific metrics are reported. No ablation or comparison against non-YOLO baselines is described.
AI.ideas_for_my_research: (1) The YOLOv5-s result (smallest model + 50 FPS) is a useful anchor for lightweight detector selection on aerial/TIR platforms, but the abstract gives no parameter/FLOPs counts, so treat it as a qualitative reference only. (2) The cross-detection analysis across UAV observation angles is a transferable evaluation protocol for your own onboard detector robustness studies. (3) The lack of deployment metrics (latency, memory, energy, edge hardware) means this paper cannot serve as evidence for onboard/in-orbit feasibility; use it only to motivate TIR-specific small-target challenges. (4) Consider whether the person/car TIR detection pipeline can be adapted to ship/vehicle targets in satellite or aerial imagery, but verify the dataset licensing and resolution gap first.
